Links: [{"title":"Long-Term Trends In The Solar Wind Proton Measurements","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/1610.06063"},{"title":"temporal and radial variation of the solar wind temperature speed","url":"https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/temporal-and-radial-variation-of-the-solar-wind-temperature-speed/"},{"title":"ACE News Archives","url":"https://izw1.caltech.edu/ACE/ACENews/ACENews143.html"},{"title":"izw1.caltech.edu","url":"https://izw1.caltech.edu/ACE/ACENews/ACENews143.pdf"},{"title":"collaborate.princeton.edu","url":"https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/temporal-and-radial-variation-of-the-solar-wind-temperature-speed/fingerprints/"},{"title":"bulk properties of the slow and fast solar wind and interplanetar","url":"https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/bulk-properties-of-the-slow-and-fast-solar-wind-and-interplanetar/"},{"title":"solar wind speed and temperature relationship","url":"https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/solar-wind-speed-and-temperature-relationship/"},{"title":"FETCH LOGICAL a5068 f34e20ce083614405b0516131ce8178803486a1d4da49b5227eb9a2b22717473","url":"https://opact.sdu.edu.tr/vufind/SummonRecord/FETCH-LOGICAL-a5068-f34e20ce083614405b0516131ce8178803486a1d4da49b5227eb9a2b22717473"},{"title":"ulysses plasma parameters latitudinal radial and temporal variati","url":"https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/ulysses-plasma-parameters-latitudinal-radial-and-temporal-variati/"}]

The search confirmed the paper and turned up its abstract. I didn't find a specific Ulysses fit parameter in these results.

- **Citation:** H. A. Elliott, C. J. Henney, D. J. McComas, C. W. Smith, and B. J. Vasquez published it in *Journal of Geophysical Research: Space Physics*, volume 117, article A09102, in 2012 (per the Princeton Research Portal record).
- **Scope:** The authors analyzed how the temperature-speed relationship of non-transient solar wind changes over time and with distance from the Sun, and they estimated a radial heating-rate profile from it.
- **Linear fit vs. distance:** The abstract says a single linear fit describes the relationship well near 1 AU, but beyond about 2.5 AU the compressions and rarefactions diverge enough that a simple linear fit no longer describes the distribution well.
- **Ulysses data:** An ACE News summary of the work says Ulysses measurements show a population of higher-temperature points starting to form around 2.5 AU, with that heated component well developed by 4 AU. It also notes that the compression and rarefaction curves separate dramatically beyond 4 AU.
- **Related work:** A 2009 JGR paper by Ebert, McComas, Elliott and colleagues, using Ulysses data, found that slow-wind proton temperature falls off less steeply with distance than fast-wind temperature. A 2016 arXiv paper (1610.06063) extends the Elliott et al. 2012 analysis and reports that the temperature-speed slope decreased from 1972 to 2010 and has increased since.

For the actual fit coefficients or Ulysses-specific equations, the full text of the 2012 paper is needed; the search results only gave the abstract and a summary.

Links: [{"title":"A review on solar wind modeling: kinetic and fluid aspects","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/1306.0704"},{"title":"ntrs.nasa.gov","url":"https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19860040981"},{"title":"EarthRef.org Reference Database (ERR)","url":"https://earthref.org/ERR/29907"},{"title":"EarthRef.org Reference Database (ERR)","url":"https://earthref.org/ERR/10028"},{"title":"earthref.org","url":"https://earthref.org/ERR/170336/"},{"title":"EarthRef.org Reference Database (ERR)","url":"https://earthref.org/ERR/169352/"},{"title":"earthref.org","url":"https://earthref.org/ERR/186575/"},{"title":"link.springer.com","url":"https://link.springer.com/doi/10.1007/BF00148530"},{"title":"earthref.org","url":"https://earthref.org/ERR/30240"},{"title":"EarthRef.org Reference Database (ERR)","url":"https://earthref.org/ERR/30280"}]

The search did not confirm the formula as you wrote it. The 1986 paper's abstract gives different coefficients, and I found no source for the 0.51V² − 142V expression.

- **Paper:** Lopez & Freeman (1986), "Solar wind proton temperature-velocity relationship," *JGR* 91, doi:10.1029/JA091iA02p01701. Data from Helios 1 are examined to find an experimental fit for the T(V) relationship at 1 AU.
- **Reported fits:** For V>500 km s-1, T=(0.77¿0.021)V-(265¿12.5), while for V<500 km s-1, T1/2=(0.031¿0.002)V-(4.39¿0.08) or T1/3=(0.0106¿0.001)V -(0.278¿0.03). The "¿" characters are encoding artifacts for ± signs.
- **Discrepancy:** Your low-speed form uses a constant of 5.1 and squares the expression. The abstract's square-root fit uses 4.39 instead. The slope of 0.031 matches.
- **Breakpoint:** The data show a distinct change in the proton temperature-velocity slope at V~500 km s-1.
- **Correction:** A 1987 erratum, "Correction to 'Solar wind proton temperature-velocity relationship,'" exists (JGR 92, doi:10.1029/JA092iA12p13679). I could not see its contents, so the 5.1 value may come from there or be a transcription difference. I'd check the erratum or the full paper before relying on either constant.
- **Other sources:** A companion paper on the proton temperature and momentum flux relationship (Lopez, Freeman & Roelof, GRL 1986) reports that in high-speed plasma (V>500 km s-1) Tp increases with increasing noV2. The NTRS record for the 1986 paper gives the same breakpoint, with the T–V form changing at a velocity of approximately 500 km/s.

I did not find the 0.51V² − 142V term in any result, so I can't confirm where it comes from.

The search found the abstract of the 1995 paper but did not confirm the r^-0.5 exponent or the heating interpretation you asked about.

**The 1995 paper:** The bibliographic record lists Richardson, Paularena, Lazarus and Belcher (1995), "Radial evolution of the solar wind from IMP 8 to Voyager 2," in *Geophysical Research Letters* 22 (Radial evolution of the solar wind from IMP 8 to Voyager 2. Geophysical Research Letters 22: doi: 10.1029/94GL03273.). Its abstract says that Voyager 2 and IMP 8 data from 1977 through 1994 are presented and compared. It also reports that radial velocity and temperature structures remain intact over the distance from 1 to 43 AU, but density structures do not. It adds that in the outer heliosphere temperature changes lead velocity changes by tens of days.

**Temperature power law:** The results did not include the paper's r^-0.5 temperature exponent or its heating discussion. Other studies in the results report different exponents. A Voyager 2 study from 1977–1978 gives the proton temperature as (-0.3 plus or minus 0.1). A separate study gives the proton temperature varies with heliocentric distance as R0.7¿0.2, but the results do not establish that this study is the 1995 paper, so I am not attributing it.

**Context:** A 1984 review by Gazis and Lazarus notes that the temperature falls more slowly than would be expected from a simple, adiabatic model. This is the background against which heating explanations are usually framed.

**Title:** Solar wind proton temperature-velocity relationship

**Authors:** R. E. Lopez (Rice University, Houston, TX) and J. W. Freeman (Rice University, Houston, TX)

**Journal:** The page does not name a journal. It lists the document type as Conference Proceedings and gives ISSN 0148-0227.

**Year:** 1986 (publication date February 1, 1986)

**Abstract:** The page's abstract is longer than the 125-character quote limit, so I can't reproduce it verbatim. In summary, the authors analyze Helios 1 data to find an experimental fit for the proton temperature-velocity relationship at 1 AU. They report that the relationship changes at about 500 km/s. They find that interplanetary processes such as stream interactions affect the relationship by less than 22 percent, and that its functional form appears to hold throughout the solar cycle. They conclude that any comprehensive solar wind model must account for the difference in this relationship between low- and high-speed wind.

A short verbatim excerpt: "the proton temperature-velocity changes at a velocity of approximately 500 km/s."

To proceed, you could:

- **Share a link or the extracted text** from the PDF of Ebert et al. (2009), McComas et al. (2000), McComas (2008), Le Chat et al. (2012), or Phillips et al. (1995).

Without the source text, I can offer general background, not sourced from this page and not quoted. Fast wind from Ulysses' polar coronal holes is typically around 750 km/s, while slow wind is around 400 km/s. Fast wind is generally less dense and hotter than slow wind. The two papers and the anticorrelation and pressure-invariance results should be checked against the originals before you rely on any of these figures.

The search located the review and its Table 1, but not the table's values. The snippets give only the table's purpose, so the actual slow and fast wind numbers at 1 au are not in these results.

- **Publication:** The review is by Verscharen, Klein, and Maruca, published in Living Reviews in Solar Physics (2019), volume 16, article 5. It was accepted in November 2019 and is open access; the DOI is 10.1007/s41116-019-0021-0 (Living Reviews in Solar Physics (2019) 16:5).
- **Table 1:** The review's section on characteristic scales says that Table 1 lists typical values for the characteristic plasma parameters and scales in the solar wind at 1 au and in the upper solar corona. The authors also note that all of these quantities vary widely in time and may differ significantly between thermal and superthermal particle populations.
- **Scope:** The abstract describes the length scales (such as the heliosphere size, collisional mean free paths, inertial lengths, gyration radii, and Debye lengths) and the timescales (such as expansion, collision, and gyration periods) (The characteristic length scales include ... The characteristic timescales include ...). It does not mention slow or fast wind specifically in these snippets.

To get the numeric table, the open-access PDF is the best route. It is available through UCL Discovery (discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10087771) and PubMed Central (PMC6934245). Those pages were returned but not opened, so I could not confirm the table's contents.
